questions.q: Why is establishing a baseline the first step in diagnosing the 7-9am timeout, before looking at any metrics?
options: Without knowing what normal (outside the window) looks like, there's nothing concrete to compare the 7-9am behavior against — "it's slow" is just a feeling without one
A baseline is a legal requirement for Azure SQL databases
Baselines are only needed for security audits, not performance work
Establishing a baseline fixes the problem automatically
questions.explain: A baseline gives the later Azure Monitor/DMV/Query Store findings something real to be compared against.

questions.q: How does this lesson say to tell a regressed query problem apart from a capacity (undersized tier) problem?
options: Query Store's regressed-queries view shows whether a specific query's plan changed for the worse; if plans look normal but Azure Monitor shows the tier maxed out during the window, that points to capacity instead
There is no reliable way to distinguish the two
Capacity problems only ever happen on Managed Instance, never on Azure SQL Database
Both problems are always fixed by adding an index
questions.explain: The two problems need different fixes — a plan/index/statistics fix for a regressed query, versus scaling the tier for a capacity ceiling.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend partitioning and compressing Telemetry now rather than waiting?
options: It's growing ~50 GB a month, and applying partitioning/compression while it's still a manageable size is materially cheaper than doing it after the table is many times larger
Partitioning is only possible on tables under 1 GB
Compression is required by DP-300 regardless of table size
Waiting has no cost difference at all
questions.explain: The storage decision is driven by the workload's growth trajectory, not a fixed rule.

questions.q: What was Meridian's actual automation problem, according to this lesson — a missing script, or something else?
options: Nothing was actively watched — jobs could fail silently for a long time, the same pattern behind the unaudited permissions Compliance flagged in Lesson 90
Meridian had no SQL Server Agent installed anywhere
The problem was that automation was too aggressive and ran too often
There was no automation problem at all
questions.explain: Scheduled jobs alone don't fix a silent-failure culture — alerts and operators are what make a failure visible instead of invisible.

questions.q: How does adopting Bicep/Infrastructure as Code for this environment directly address a specific concern the CFO raised in Lesson 90?
options: It lets the environment's configuration be rebuilt or audited from code instead of manual portal work, moving away from treating infrastructure as a recurring one-off hardware purchase
Bicep automatically reduces Azure compute costs by half
Bicep replaces the need for any security controls
It has no connection to anything the CFO said
questions.explain: The CFO's Lesson 90 concern was about repeated capital hardware spend and unpredictable cost — IaC is the concrete, code-based answer to operating the environment differently going forward.
